narrative:
The model predicted an 88.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and this probability is so high, your application was rejected.

The three factors that mattered most to this decision were your class ranking in your third year of law school, your LSAT score, and your undergraduate GPA. Your third-year ranking was by far the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile (compared to an average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students) signaled that you struggled to keep pace with your classmates later in the program. Your LSAT score was the second-biggest driver and also pulled the outcome toward failure; a score of 25 is well below the average of 37 seen among students who were admitted. These two weaknesses outweighed the one positive factor, your undergraduate GPA of 3.5, which is actually higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore worked in your favor, though not enough to change the overall result.

Your family income and plan to attend full-time were not major factors in the decision.

To improve your chances next time, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise that score. A stronger showing in those two areas would likely shift future predictions in your favor. (218 words)
